name: Lavender oil capsules (Silexan)
lead: Silexan is a standardized oral lavender oil preparation sold as 80 mg capsules for anxiety and restlessness. It is made from Lavandula angustifolia flowers and is marketed in Germany as a medicine and in the US as a supplement (CalmAid).[1][8]

People who take it for their looks do so by way of calmer mood and better sleep: less anxiety and restlessness can mean better sleep, which proponents associate with clearer skin, less puffiness around the eyes and more energy for training. Silexan itself has no studied appearance effect; its research is about anxiety, sleep and mood.[8][15]

Placebo-controlled trials of 80 mg daily over about ten weeks reported reduced anxiety symptoms, and a 2010 randomised trial compared it with lorazepam in generalized anxiety disorder.[10][11][12] The NCCIH, as summarised on Wikipedia, states that the effectiveness of oral lavender for anxiety is not established, and the product is distinct from lavender aromatherapy or topical lavender oil.[1] Lavender oil is toxic if swallowed in large amounts, especially for children.[1]

paras: Lavender oil is distilled from flower spikes and is among the most commonly adulterated essential oils, according to a reference page.[1] Reviews of its biological activities describe antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory laboratory findings alongside traditional calming uses.[2][3] A laboratory study of 21 plant extracts also tested anti-collagenase and anti-elastase activity.[3] Silexan is a specific, standardized oral product distinct from topical or aromatherapy oils; reviews describe it as a lavender oil preparation available in 80 mg capsules.[8] Constituents of lavender oil include linalool and linalyl acetate.[1][2]

A narrative review of seven clinical trials found that in patients with subthreshold or generalized anxiety, an anxiolytic effect was evident after two weeks, with reductions in Hamilton Anxiety scale scores superior to placebo in subthreshold anxiety and comparable to lorazepam or paroxetine in generalized anxiety disorder.[8] A pooled analysis of three placebo-controlled trials in subthreshold anxiety gave 80 mg daily or placebo for ten weeks and measured anxiety, sleep quality and quality of life.[10] A 2010 multicentre, double-blind randomised study compared Silexan with lorazepam in generalized anxiety disorder.[11] A 2025 review summarises six studies in anxiety and mixed anxiety and depression and reports comparability with lorazepam 0.5 mg and paroxetine 20 mg, and in mild to moderate depression with sertraline 50 mg.[12][13]

A 2022 network meta-analysis of 29 trials comparing 12 medicinal herbs found Silexan displayed a significant effect on anxiety (mean difference -3.84 on the Hamilton scale), and possibly benefited depression and insomnia.[9] A 2026 network meta-analysis of 100 trials noted silexan as the only phytopharmaceutical included.[19] The NCCIH states that aromatherapy and topical lavender have no established clinical benefit and that oral effectiveness for anxiety is undetermined; a 2022 guideline suggested it may be useful in depression.[1]

A randomised trial analysis reported that Silexan's beneficial effects on sleep were mediated by its anxiolytic effect, and a narrative review summarises its effect on sleep quality.[15][20] This is the main route by which people expect it to influence how rested they look.

The FDA lists lavender oil as generally recognized as safe for its intended uses. Swallowing about 5 mL of diluted essential oil may cause toxicity in adults and 2 to 3 mL in children, and New South Wales recorded 271 reported poisonings in 2014 to 2018, mostly in children. Topical use can cause contact dermatitis, and ingestion may interact with anticoagulants, statins and anticonvulsants. Lavender oil is described as a potential endocrine disruptor.[1] A randomised trial reported that Silexan did not cause withdrawal symptoms when abruptly discontinued.[14]

Silexan is sold in the US as the supplement CalmAid and in Germany as the medicine Lasea.[1] Hacker News carried a 2022 discussion titled Lavender's Game: Silexan for Anxiety.[18] On T Nation, a thread on anxiety shared a CalmAid softgel product link, and another thread listed it among herbs asked about for organ effects.[17][21]

Controlled trials of oral Silexan in anxiety, depression and sleep are summarised above.[8][10][11][13] A 2019 meta-analysis of lavender in any form (including aromatherapy) assessed anxiety outcomes across randomised and non-randomised studies.[16] Separate registered trials of inhaled lavender aromatherapy test anxiety and pain around medical procedures, in dental settings and in hemodialysis.[4][5][6] A study in a dental office found ambient lavender and orange odors reduced anxiety and improved mood.[7] These involve inhalation, not oral Silexan. No studies of oral lavender for appearance were found.

lore.intro: Silexan appears occasionally in supplement and stress-management discussion on T Nation and Hacker News rather than as a mainstream looksmaxxing topic.[17][18]

claims.claim: A calming lavender capsule can take the edge off anxiety without sedation.
claims.believers: Posters share a non-drowsy Silexan softgel product and ask about it as an anxiety option alongside other supplements.[17]
claims.experts: Reviews of Silexan trials report anxiolytic effects versus placebo and comparability with lorazepam or paroxetine in some trials, while the NCCIH states oral effectiveness is not established.[8][12][1]

claims.claim: Better sleep and lower stress from it will show up in skin and appearance.
claims.believers: The idea follows from supplement-forum reasoning that anxiety and poor sleep affect how rested and healthy a person looks.[17]
claims.experts: Trials measure anxiety and sleep scores; no published study has measured skin or appearance after oral lavender.[15][8]

card.summary: Standardized oral lavender oil sold for anxiety; some placebo-controlled data, no appearance use.
card.note: Essential oil is toxic if swallowed in quantity, especially by children.

quick.overview:
Silexan is a capsule containing a standardized lavender oil, taken for anxiety and restlessness.
Controlled trials report reduced anxiety, though the NCCIH says oral effectiveness is not established. It has no studied appearance use.
quick.mechanism: Linalool and linalyl acetate are the main constituents. How the oral product acts is not settled.
quick.risks: Pure lavender oil is toxic if swallowed in quantity, with poisonings reported mostly in children. Topical oil can cause contact dermatitis, and interactions with some drugs have been noted.

angle.text: People who use Silexan for appearance reasons do so for its calming and sleep-related effects, expecting rested, less tense looks as a downstream result.[15][17] The published research measures anxiety, depression and sleep scores rather than skin or appearance.
